Surah 93: al-Duha (The Morning Brightness)
Eleven verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the morning brightness﴾ ﴿and by the night when it is still﴾

I am determined to add to my tafsir (exegesis) of this surah the subtle reminders it contains.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the morning brightness﴾ ﴿and by the night when it is still﴾. Concerning His saying ﴿By the morning brightness﴾, the exegetes have two views:

The first: the intended meaning of "al-duha" is the time of forenoon, which is the early part of the day, when the sun rises and casts its rays.

The second: al-duha is the whole day, as evidence that it is set in contrast to the whole night.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and by the night when it is still﴾, the lexicographers mention three closely related meanings for ﴿sajā﴾: it became still, it grew dark, and it covered.

As for the first: Abu 'Ubayd, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: "sajā" means "it became still." One says "a still night" (laylah sājiyah), meaning a night with calm wind, and "a languid eye" (ʿayn sājiyah), meaning an eye with drooping glance. The sea "sajā" when its waves become calm. And in supplication one says:

"O Master of the sea when the sea is still."

As for the second, which interprets "sajā" as "grew dark": al-Farrā' said: "sajā" means it grew dark and remained stationary throughout its length.

As for the third, which interprets "sajā" as "covered": al-Asma'i and Ibn al-A'rabi said: the night "sajā" means it covers the day, just as a man is covered (yusajjā) with a garment. Know that the statements of the exegetes do not go outside these three meanings. Ibn 'Abbas said: it covered the world with darkness. al-Hasan said: people were clothed in its darkness. Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, said: when the night comes, it covers everything. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: it became still with the people, and its stillness has two meanings:

The first: the stillness of the people, so it is attributed to the night, as one says "a sleeping night" and "a fasting day."

The second: its stillness is an expression for the settling of its darkness

[Page 189]

and its becoming level, so that it does not increase after that. Here there are questions.

The first question: What is the wisdom in that He, exalted is He, mentioned the night first in the previous surah, but delayed it in this surah? We say: there are several reasons.

The first: the interests of the responsible persons (mukallafin) are arranged by night and day. The night has the merit of precedence, as in His saying ﴿He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. The day has the merit of light. Indeed, the night is like this world and the day is like the Hereafter. Since each has a merit that the other does not have, it is necessarily the case that this is sometimes mentioned before that, and that sometimes before this. A parallel is that He, exalted is He, put prostration before bowing in His saying ﴿O Mary, prostrate yourself and bow down﴾ [Al 'Imran: 43], then put bowing before prostration in His saying ﴿Bow down and prostrate yourselves﴾ [al-Hajj: 77].

The second: He, exalted is He, put the night before the day in the Surah of Abu Bakr, because Abu Bakr had preceded disbelief. Here He put the morning brightness first, because the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, had never been preceded by sin.

The third: the Surah of "By the night" is the Surah of Abu Bakr, and the Surah of the morning brightness is the Surah of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. Then nothing was placed between them, to make known that there is no intermediary between Muhammad and Abu Bakr. So when you mention the night first, which is Abu Bakr, then ascend, you find after it the day, which is Muhammad. And if you mention "the morning brightness" first, which is Muhammad, then descend, you find after it the night, which is Abu Bakr, so that it is known that there is no intermediary between the two.

The second question: What is the wisdom here in swearing only by the morning brightness and the night?

The answer: for several reasons.

The first: it is as if He, exalted is He, says: time is an hour; so an hour is an hour of night and an hour of day. Then it increases, so that at one time the hours of night increase and the hours of day decrease, and at another time it is the reverse. Thus the increase is not from desire, nor the decrease from hatred, but from wisdom. Likewise, prophethood and the sending down of revelation occur according to interests: at one time there is sending down and at another time there is withholding. So the sending down was not from desire, nor the withholding from hatred.

The second: the scholar's words have no effect until he acts upon them. When Allah, exalted is He, commanded that the proof is upon the claimant and the oath upon the one who denies, He had no choice but to act upon it Himself. So when the disbelievers claimed that his Lord had abandoned him and hated him, He said: "Bring your proof." They were unable, so the oath became incumbent on Him that He had not abandoned him and had not hated him.

The third: it is as if He, exalted is He, says: look at the neighboring of night with day: neither of them is free from the other, but night sometimes prevails and sometimes is overcome. How, then, do you hope to be safe among creation?!

The third question: Why was the time of the morning brightness singled out for mention?

The answer: there are several reasons.

The first: it is the time of people gathering and of full intimacy after loneliness during the night. So they gave him good news that after his loneliness caused by the withholding of revelation, the morning brightness of the descent of revelation would appear.

The second: it is the hour in which Moses spoke with his Lord, and in which the magicians were cast down prostrating, so the time took on the attribute of merit by being a container (zarf). How then does one who performs obedience...! It also conveys that He who honored Moses will not abandon honoring you, and He who turned the hearts of the magicians until they prostrated will turn the hearts of your enemies.

The fourth question: What is the reason that He mentioned the morning brightness, which is an hour of the day, but mentioned the night in its entirety?

The answer: there are several reasons.

The first: it is an indication that an hour of the day is equal to all of the night, just as Muhammad, if weighed, equals all the prophets.

The second: the day is the time of joy and ease, and the night is the time of loneliness and grief. So this indicates that the cares of this world are more lasting than its joys, for the morning brightness is one hour while the night is many hours. It is narrated that when Allah, exalted is He, created the Throne, a black cloud shaded from its left and called out: "What shall I rain?" It was answered: "Rain cares and sorrows for a hundred years." Then it dispersed, and it was commanded again in the same way, and so on until three hundred years were completed. After that, a white cloud shaded from the right of the Throne and called: "What shall I rain?" It was answered: "Rain joy for an hour." Therefore, for this reason you see sorrows and griefs lasting, and joy scarce and rare.

[Page 190]

The third: the time of the morning brightness is the time of people's movement and mutual acquaintance, so it becomes like the time of resurrection, while the night, when it becomes still, is like the stillness of people in the darkness of graves. Both are wisdom and blessing, but the superiority belongs to life over death. Since death is far from what precedes it, for this reason He mentioned the morning brightness before the mention of the night.

The fourth: He mentioned the morning brightness so that despair would not arise from His spirit, and then followed it with the night so that security from His plan would not arise.

The fifth question: Has any of those mentioned interpreted "the morning brightness" as the face of Muhammad and "the night" as his hair? The answer: Yes, and there is no improbability in it. Among them is one who added to this, saying: "The morning brightness" refers to the males of his household, and "the night" to its females. It is also possible: "the morning brightness" is his prophethood, and "the night" is the time of the withholding of revelation, because during the time of descent there was companionship, and during the time of withholding there was loneliness. It is also possible that "the morning brightness" is the light of His knowledge, by which the hidden of the unseen is known, and "the night" is His pardon, by which He covers all faults. It is also possible that the morning brightness is the rising of Islam after it had been strange, and "the night" is an indication that it will return to being strange. It is also possible that "the morning brightness" is the perfection of intellect, and "the night" is the state of death. It is also possible: I swear by your openness, in which the creatures see no fault, and by your secret, in which the Knower of the unseen finds no fault.

[Page 188]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 93, verse 3:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your Lord has not bid you farewell, nor has He detested you.﴾ On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Abu 'Ubayda and al-Mubarrad said: *wadda'aka* (ودَّعَكَ) comes from *al-taw'id* (التَّوْدِيع), as one bids farewell to someone who is departing. It has also been recited with the lightened form (*bi-l-takhfif*), meaning *ma taraka-ka* (ما تَرَكَكَ), "He has not left you." *Al-taw'id* is an intensification of *al-wada'* (farewell), because one who bids you farewell as a departing person has gone to the extreme of abandoning you. *Al-qila* (القِلى) means hatred. It is said: *qalahu yaqlihi qila* and *maqliyya* (قَلاهُ يَقْلِيهِ قِلًى ومَقْلِيَةً) when he hated him. Al-Farra' said: "It means *wa ma qalaka*," i.e., "nor has He detested you." Concerning the omission of the *kaf* (the pronoun "you") there are several explanations:

First: The *kaf* is omitted because the first *kaf* in *wadda'aka* suffices, and because the verse endings (*ru'us al-ayat*, i.e., *fawasil*, the rhyming endings of verses) end in *ya'*, so the agreement of the endings required the omission of the *kaf*.

Second: The benefit of the unrestricted form is that He has not detested you, nor has He detested any of your companions, nor anyone who has loved you until the Day of Resurrection. This confirms his saying (ﷺ): "A person is with whom he loves."

**The second issue:** The exegetes said: Gabriel was delayed in coming to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the polytheists said: "Allah has detested him and bid him farewell." Then Allah revealed this verse to him. Al-Suddi said: He was delayed for forty nights, and he complained of this to Khadija, who said: "Perhaps your Lord has forgotten you, or has detested you." It is also reported that Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab, said to him: "O Muhammad, I do not see your devil except that he has left you." It is reported from al-Hasan that he said: The revelation was delayed from the Messenger (ﷺ), so he said to Khadija: "My Lord has bid me farewell and has detested me," complaining to her. She said: "No indeed, by He who sent you with the truth, Allah did not begin with you this honour except that He intends to complete it for you." Then there was revealed: ﴿Your Lord has not bid you farewell, nor has He detested you.﴾

The scholars of foundational principles (*usuliyyun*, i.e., theologians) criticised this narration. They said: It is not fitting for the Messenger (ﷺ) to suppose that Allah, exalted is He, had bid him farewell and detested him. Rather, he knows that removing the Prophet from prophethood is not permissible in the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, and he knows that the descent of revelation occurs according to what is beneficial, and perhaps the good lies in delaying it, and perhaps it lies in the opposite. Thus it is established that this statement is not fitting for the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. Then, if it is authentic, it is interpreted to mean that his intention, upon him be blessings and peace, was to test her (Khadija) in order to know the extent of her knowledge, or so that people might know the extent of her knowledge.

They differed on the length of the interruption of revelation. Ibn Jurayj said: twelve days. Al-Kalbi said: fifteen days. Ibn 'Abbas said: twenty-five days. Al-Suddi and Muqatil said: forty days.

[p. 191]

They differed on the cause of Gabriel's (peace be upon him) withholding. Most exegetes mention that the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the Spirit (*al-Ruh*), Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and the People of the Cave. He said: "I will inform you tomorrow," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him. Ibn Zayd said: The cause was a puppy in the house belonging to al-Hasan and al-Husayn. When Gabriel (peace be upon him) came down, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) rebuked him, and he said: "Do you not know that we do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture?" Jundub ibn Sufyan said: "The Prophet (peace be upon him) was struck by a stone on his finger, and he said: 'Are you not but a finger that bleeds, and in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered?' So revelation was delayed from him." It is also reported that there were among them (the people of the household) those who did not trim their nails.

Here there are two questions.

**The first question:** Do the narrations you have mentioned indicate that the withholding of revelation was out of detestation? (We say:) The most that can be said on this matter is that it was the abandonment of what is better and preferable, and one who does this is not detestable or hated. It is reported that he (peace be upon him) said to Gabriel: "You did not come to me until I longed for you." Gabriel said: "I was more longing for you, but I am a commanded servant." And he recited: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64].

**The second question:** How is it proper for a sovereign to say to the one closest to him in nearness: "I do not hate you," in order to honour him? The answer: This is not proper at the outset. But when enemies spread in the tongues that the sovereign hates him, and then that intimate becomes distressed, there is no expression closer to honouring him than to say to him: "I do not hate you, nor do I abandon you, and you will see your station with me."

**The third issue:** This event indicates that the Qur'an is from Allah, for had it been from him (Muhammad), it would not have prohibited (such a statement).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 93, verse 4:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾.

Know that concerning its connection to what precedes, there are several views.

The first: the meaning is that the cessation of revelation (*wahy*) cannot be because He has dismissed you from prophethood. Rather, at most, the matter is that you have come to need no further message, and that is a sign of death. So it is as if it were said: the cessation of revelation, whenever it occurs, indicates death. But death is better for you, for what you have with Allah in the Hereafter is better and more excellent than what you have in this world.

The second: when there was revealed ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾, he received through this a great honour. It is as if he regarded this honour as very great, so it was said to him: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾, meaning: this honour, though great, is less than what you have with Allah in the Hereafter, which is better and greater.

The third, which occurs to my mind, is that the meaning is: and the coming states are better for you than the past ones. It is as if He, exalted is He, promised him that He would increase him each day in honour upon honour and rank upon rank. So He says: Do not think that I have forsaken you; rather, every day that comes you will be (higher), for I will increase you in rank and majesty. Here there are two questions.

The first question: By what means is it known that the Hereafter is better for him than the first (life)? The answer: for several reasons.

The first: it is as if He, exalted is He, says to him: You are upon good in this world because you do in it what you wish; but the Hereafter is better for you because We do in it what We wish.

The second: the Hereafter is better for you, in that your community (*ummah*) gathers around you, for the community is to him like children. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and he is their father. His community will be in Paradise, so it is as if his children are in Paradise. Then He called the child "coolness of the eyes," where He related of them: ﴿Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort of our eyes﴾ [al-Furqan: 74].

The third: the Hereafter is better for you because you have purchased it, whereas this (world) is not yours. Supposing the Hereafter were less than this world, the Hereafter would still be better for you, because what is owned by you is better for you than what is not owned by you. So how much more so, when there is no comparison between the Hereafter and this world in excellence.

The fourth: the Hereafter is better for you than the first, because in this world the disbelievers revile you, but in the Hereafter I will make your community witnesses over the nations, and I will make you a witness over the prophets. Then I will make My own Essence a witness for you, as He said: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 28, 29].

The fifth: the good things of this world are few, mixed, and transient, while the delights of the Hereafter are abundant, pure, and everlasting.

The second question: Why did He say: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you﴾ and not "better for you all"?

The answer: because among his company were those for whom the Hereafter would be evil. Had He, glory be to Him, generalised, it would have been a lie. And had He singled out only the obedient for mention, the sinners and the hypocrites would have been exposed. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Nay, indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. As for Muhammad (ﷺ), those who were with him were, by certainty, among the people of felicity, so, undoubtedly, he said: ﴿Indeed Allah is with us﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], since there was none there except a prophet and a truthful one (*siddiq*).

It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, went out to seek rain, and with him were thousands, for three days, but they were not answered. So Moses, peace be upon him, asked about the cause that prevented the answer. He was told: "I will not answer you as long as there is among you one who goes about with tale-bearing." Moses asked: "Who is he?" He (the answer) said: "I hate him, so how can I do his deed?" Not long passed before revelation came down that this tale-bearer had died, and that his funeral was in such-and-such a prayer-place. Moses, peace be upon him, went to that prayer-place, and there were seventy biers in it. So this is His concealment of His enemies; how much more, then, of His friends.

Then reflect, for there is in it a subtle point: he, peace be upon him, said: "Had it not been for the bowing elders..." and in this is an indication of the increased excellence of this community. For He, exalted is He, would turn back thousands because of one sinner, whereas here He shows mercy to the sinners for the sake of one obedient person.

[p. 192]

The Lord's Words: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾. Know its connection to what precedes it in two ways:

The first: when He, exalted is He, explained that the Hereafter is "better for you than the first (life)," He did not explain to what extent that difference would reach. So with this verse He explained the measure of that difference: it extends to the utmost of what the Messenger (ﷺ) wishes for and is pleased with.

The second: it is as if He, exalted is He, when He said ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾, was asked, "Why did you say the matter is so?" And He said: "Because He will give him everything he desires, and that is something the world cannot contain." Thus it is established that the Hereafter is better for him than this world. Know that if we take this promise to refer to the Hereafter, it may be taken to refer to benefits, and it may be taken to refer to honour. As for benefits, Ibn 'Abbas said: "A thousand palaces in Paradise of white pearl, their dust is musk, and in them is whatever befits them." As for honour, what is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and from Ibn 'Abbas is that this is intercession (shafa'ah) for the Ummah. It is related that when this verse was revealed, he (peace be upon him) said: "Then I will not be satisfied while a single one of my Ummah is in the Fire." Know that taking it to mean intercession is the definite reading, and several points indicate this:

One: He, exalted is He, commanded him in this world to seek forgiveness, saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. So He commanded him to seek forgiveness, and seeking forgiveness is an expression for asking for forgiveness. Whoever asks for something, there is no doubt that he does not want it refused, nor is he pleased with refusal, but rather he is pleased with its being granted. When it is established that what the Messenger (ﷺ) is pleased with is the granting and not the refusal, and this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, gives him everything he is pleased with, we know that this verse indicates intercession on behalf of those who have committed sins.

Two: The preceding part of the verse is suitable for this. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "I will not abandon you, nor will I hate you; rather, I will not be angry with any of your companions, followers and supporters, seeking your pleasure and comforting your heart." So this is more fitting to the preceding part of the verse.

Three: The many hadiths that come concerning intercession indicate that the pleasure of the Messenger, peace be upon him, lies in pardoning those who have committed sins. This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, does everything that the Messenger is pleased with. So from the combination of the verse and the report, the occurrence of intercession is established. It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, that he said: "The pleasure of my grandfather is that no monotheist enters the Fire." And from al-Baqir: "The people of the Qur'an say: the most hopeful verse is His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [Az-Zumar: 53]. But we, the People of the House, say: the most hopeful verse is His saying: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾. By Allah, it is indeed intercession, which will be given concerning the people of 'There is no god but Allah', until he says, 'I am satisfied.'"

All of this is when we take the verse to refer to the conditions of the Hereafter. But if we take this promise to refer to the conditions of this world, then it is an allusion to what Allah, exalted is He, granted him: victory over his enemies on the Day of Badr and the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, the entry of people into the religion in multitudes, dominance over Qurayzah and al-Nadir and their expulsion, the dispatch of his armies and expeditions into the lands of the Arabs, what He opened to his rightly-guided successors in the regions of the earth of cities, what they demolished with their hands of the kingdoms of tyrants, what they plundered of the treasures of the Chosroes, and the terror cast into the people of East and West, the awe of Islam, and the spread of the call. Know that the better view is to take the verse as referring to the good things of this world and the Hereafter together. Here there are questions:

The first question: Why did He not say "will give you" (plural), given that these felicities were also attained by the believers?

The answer: for several reasons.

One: that is the intended meaning, and they are followers.

Two: when I honour your companions, that is in reality an honour to you, because I know that you have gone so far in compassion for them that you are happier with their honour than with the honour of yourself. From this is that when the prophets say, "Myself, myself," meaning, "Begin with my reward and my recompense before my Ummah, for my obedience came before the obedience of my Ummah," you say, "My Ummah, my Ummah," meaning, "Begin with them, for my joy is that I see them triumphant with their reward."

Three: you dealt with me in a good manner. When they wounded your face, you said: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know." And when they distracted you from the prayer on the Day of the Trench, you said: "O Allah, fill their bellies with fire." So you bore the wound inflicted on the face of your body, but you did not bear the wound inflicted on the face of your religion, for the face of religion is the prayer. So you preferred my right over your right. Therefore, I have favoured you, and I said: whoever abandons prayer for years, or prevents another from prayer for years, I will not expiate it for him; and whoever harms a single hair of yours, or a part of your sandal, I will expiate it.

The second question: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿sawfa﴾ ("will"), and why did He not say "wa-sa-yu'tika" ("and your Lord will give you")?

The answer: there are benefits in it.

One of them: it indicates that his death had not drawn near, but that he would live a period of time after that.

Second: when the polytheists said, "His Lord has farewelled him and abandoned him," Allah, exalted is He, replied to them with the very same word, saying: ﴿Your Lord has not farewelled you, nor has He abandoned you﴾. Then the polytheists said, "Muhammad will die" (sawfa yamutu), so Allah replied to them with this same word, saying: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾.

The third question: How can Allah say ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾?

The answer: this entire surah, from its beginning to its end, is the speech of Jibril, peace be upon him, with him, because he was intensely eager for him and for his speech, as we mentioned. So Allah, exalted is He, wanted him to be the one who addresses him with these glad tidings.

The fourth question: What is this lam that enters upon "sawfa"?

The answer: The author of the "Kashshaf" said: it is the lam of inception (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam that begins a sentence), which emphasises the content of the sentence, and the subject is omitted, its estimated form being: "Indeed, you (are the one to whom) your Lord will surely give." The evidence for what we have said is that it is either the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) or the lam of inception. The lam of oath does not enter upon the present-tense verb except with the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid), so it remains that it is the lam of inception. The lam of inception only enters upon a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate, so it is necessary to estimate a subject and predicate, and its original form would be: "Indeed you, He will surely give you." If it is asked: what is the meaning of combining two emphatic particles, the lam and the postponement (sawfa)? We say: its meaning is that the giving is certain to happen, even if it is delayed, because of the benefit in the delay.

**Verse 6 of Surah 93:** ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾

Al-Razi says: There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** Its connection with what came before is that God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan?﴾ The Messenger replies: "Yes, my Lord." Then God says: "Consider: were your acts of obedience at that time more honourable, or now?" It must be said: "Now." God then says: "When you were a weak infant, We did not abandon you. Rather, We raised you and elevated you until you stood overlooking the battlements of the Throne, and We said to you: 'Were it not for you, We would not have created the spheres.' Do you suppose that after this state We would forsake you and leave you?"

**The second issue:** ﴿Did He not find you﴾ is from *wujūd* in the sense of *ʿilm* (knowing). The two accusative nouns are the two objects of *wajada*, and the finding is from God. The meaning is: "Did God not know you to be an orphan and give you refuge?" Regarding the interpretation of *yatīm* (orphan), they mention two points.

*The first:* According to what the historians have related, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib died while the mother of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was pregnant with him. Then the Messenger of God was born, and he was with his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and with his mother Āmina. His mother Āmina died when he was six years old, so he was with his grandfather. Then his grandfather died two years after his mother, when the Messenger of God was eight years old. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib used to entrust him to Abū Ṭālib, because ʿAbd Allāh and Abū Ṭālib were from the same mother. Abū Ṭālib was the one who sponsored the Messenger of God after his grandfather, until God sent him with prophethood, and he supported him for a long period. Then Abū Ṭālib died after that, and no orphanhood at all appeared to be upon the Messenger of God. So God reminded him of this blessing.

It is related that Abū Ṭālib once said to his brother al-ʿAbbās: "Shall I not tell you about Muḥammad, of what I have seen from him?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I took him to me, and how could I not part from him for an hour of night or day? I did not entrust him to anyone, to the extent that I would have him sleep on my bed. One night I commanded him to take off his clothes and sleep with me. I saw dislike in his face, but he disliked to oppose me, and he said: 'O uncle, turn your face away from me until I take off my clothes, for it is not fitting for anyone to look at my body.' I was amazed at his words and turned my sight away until he entered the bed. When I entered the bed with him, there was a garment between me and him—by God, I had not put it on his bed—and he was in the utmost softness and fragrance, as if he had been dipped in musk. I strove to look at his body, but I could not see anything. Often I would miss him from my bed, and when I rose to look for him, he would call out: 'Here I am, uncle, come back.' I often heard from him words that pleased me, at the passing of the night. We did not say the name of God over food and drink, nor did we praise Him after them. He used to say at the beginning of his meal: 'In the name of God, the One.' When he finished his meal he said: 'Praise be to God.' I was amazed by him. Then I never saw from him a lie, nor laughter, nor ignorance, nor did he stop with children playing."

Know that the wondrous reports related concerning him, such as the narration of the monk Baḥīrā and others, are well known.

*The second interpretation of yatīm:* it is from the expression "a unique pearl" (*durra yatīma*), and the meaning is: "Did He not find you singular among Quraysh, without equal, and give you refuge?" That is, He made for you someone to whom you could turn, namely Abū Ṭālib.

It is also read *fa-āwā* (فَآوى), and this has two meanings: either it is from *awāhu* meaning *āwāhu* (he gave him shelter), or from *awā lahu* when he showed him mercy. Here there are two questions.

**The first question:** How is it fitting for generosity to bestow a favour and say: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ What confirms this question is that God, exalted is He, related of Pharaoh that he said: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 18], in the context of blaming Pharaoh. So if this was blameworthy in Pharaoh, how can it be fitting from God?

*The answer:* This is fitting when the intention is to strengthen his heart and promise him the continuation of the blessing. By this the difference becomes clear between this kind of bestowing-favour and the bestowing-favour of Pharaoh. For the bestowing-favour of Pharaoh nullifies (the good), because its aim is: "So what is the matter with you that you do not serve me?" But God's bestowing-favour is by increasing His blessings, as if He were saying: "What is wrong with you that you cut off your hope from Me? Did I not begin your upbringing? Do you think I would abandon what I have done? Rather, I must complete My blessing upon you and upon your community, as He said: ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150]. Do you not know that a pregnant woman who miscarries the child before its completion is blameworthy and is rebuked? If she miscarries, or a man causes her to miscarry by treatment, the *ghurra* (blood-money for the fetus, a technical term meaning the compensation due for a miscarried fetus) becomes obligatory and she deserves blame. So how could this be fitting from the Living, the Self-Subsisting?" How great is the difference between a bestower who is God and a bestower who is Pharaoh!

A parallel to this is what some said: ﴿They are three, their fourth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], about that earlier community, and about the community of Muḥammad: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujādila: 7]. So vast is the difference between a community whose fourth is their dog and a community whose fourth is their Lord!

**The second question:** God bestowed three favours upon him, then commanded him to mention the blessing of his Lord. What is the connection between these things?

*The answer:* The connection is this. We say: repaying a debt is obligatory. Debts are of two kinds: financial and beneficent. The second is stronger in obligation, because the financial debt may be dropped by release, whereas the second becomes more binding by release. The financial debt is paid once, and a person is freed from it; the second is obligatory for you to repay throughout your life. Then, if it is impossible to repay a small blessing from a benefactor who is himself a creature, what then of a great blessing from a great Benefactor? It is as if the servant says: "My God, You brought me from non-existence into existence as a sound human, outwardly pure but inwardly impure. It is a good tiding from You that You would cover my sins with the covering of Your pardon, as You covered my impurity with the outer skin. How then can I repay Your blessing, which has no limit and no bound?" God, exalted is He, says: "The way to that is that you do toward My servants what I have done toward you. You were an orphan and I gave you refuge, so do that toward orphans. You were astray and I guided you, so do that toward My servants. You were poor and I enriched you, so do that toward My servants." Then, if you do all of that, know that you have done it only by My enabling you, by My kindness, and by My guidance. So always be mindful of these blessings and graces.

[p. 196]

As for His saying, ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾, know that some people held that he was a disbeliever at the outset, and then God guided him and made him a prophet. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means: a disbeliever among a misguided people, so He guided you to monotheism. Al-Suddi said: he was upon the religion of his people for forty years. Mujahid said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means lost from guidance to His religion. They supported this with other verses, among them His saying, ﴿You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shura 42:52], and His saying, ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ [Yusuf 12:3], and His saying, ﴿If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]. This indicates the possibility of this from him. Since this verse indicates the possibility, His saying ﴿And He found you lost﴾ must be read in accordance with it. As for the majority of scholars,

[p. 196 continued]
they agreed that he, peace be upon him, never disbelieved in God for a single moment. Then the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: this is not permissible by reason, because it involves repelling people from him. But according to our companions, this is not impossible by reason, because it is conceivable that a person was a disbeliever, and then God grants him faith and honours him with prophethood. However, the transmitted proof has established that this possibility did not occur, namely His saying, ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm 53:2]. Then they mentioned many interpretations of this verse:

The first: what has been narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Shahr ibn Hawshab: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means: unaware of the landmarks of blessing and the rulings of the law, heedless of them, so He guided you to them. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was﴾, and His saying, ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾.

The second: he strayed from his wet-nurse Halimah when she wanted to return him to his grandfather, until she entered [the temple of] Hubal and complained to it about this, and the idols fell down, and she heard a voice saying: "Our destruction is at the hand of this boy." There is a lengthy account of this.

The third: what has been narrated as a report traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "I strayed from my grandfather Abd al-Muttalib when I was a young child, lost, and hunger nearly killed me, so God guided me." Al-Dahhak mentioned this, and mentioned his clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and his saying:

"O Lord, return my son Muhammad to me,
Return him, my Lord, and do a kindness for me."

He kept repeating this at the House until Abu Jahl came to him on a she-camel, with Muhammad before him, and [Abu Jahl] said: "We do not know what we should make of your son." Abd al-Muttalib said: "Why?" He said: "I made the she-camel kneel and had him ride behind me, but the she-camel refused to stand. When I had him ride in front of me, the she-camel stood up, as if the she-camel were saying: 'You fool, he is the leader, so how can he ride behind the one who follows?'" Ibn Abbas said: God returned him to his grandfather through the hand of his enemy, just as He did with Musa when He preserved him through the hand of his enemy.

The fourth: when he, peace be upon him, went out with Khadijah's servant Maysarah, a disbeliever seized the reins of his camel until it strayed, so God sent Jibril, peace be upon him, in the form of a human, and he guided him to the caravan. It is also said that Abu Talib took him out to Syria, and he strayed from the road, and God guided him.

The fifth: it is said: "The water got lost in the milk" when it becomes submerged. So the meaning of the verse is: you were submerged among the disbelievers in Makkah, and God strengthened you until you made His religion manifest.

The sixth: the Arabs call a lone tree in the desert "dallah" (a solitary one). It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: those lands were like a desert with no tree bearing the fruit of faith in God and knowledge of Him except you. So you were a unique tree in the desert of ignorance, and He found you lost from knowledge of God, exalted is He, when you were a young child, as He said: ﴿And God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78]. Then He created in you reason, guidance and knowledge. What is meant by "lost" is one empty of knowledge, not one characterised by a mistaken belief.

The eighth: you were lost regarding prophethood; you did not hope for it, nor did anything of it occur to your heart. The Jews and Christians used to claim that prophethood was among the Children of Israel, so I guided you to prophethood, which you had absolutely never hoped for.

The ninth: the address may be to the leader while the intended people are his folk. So His saying ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means: He found your people lost, so He guided them through you and through your law.

The tenth: He found you lost among the lost, isolated from them, withdrawn from their religion. The further you were from them, the greater their misguidance was, so He guided you to mix with them and to call them to the clear religion.

The eleventh: He found you lost regarding the migration, bewildered in the hand of the Quraysh, wishing to be parted from them, and you could not leave without His permission. So when He permitted it, and the Siddiq (Abu Bakr) agreed with him, He guided him to the tent of Umm Ma'bad. What happened with the story of Suraqah, and the manifestation of strength in the religion, was what was meant by His saying, ﴿and He guided﴾.

The twelfth: lost regarding the qiblah, for he used to wish that the Ka'bah be made his qiblah, and he did not know whether that would be granted to him. So God guided him by His saying: ﴿So We shall surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:144]. It is as if that bewilderment was called "going astray".

The thirteenth: when Jibril, peace be upon him, appeared to him at the beginning of his matter, he did not know whether it was Jibril or not, and he feared him greatly, and perhaps he wanted to throw himself from the mountain. So God guided him until he knew that it was Jibril, peace be upon him.

The fourteenth: "dalal" (going astray) in the sense of love, as in His saying: ﴿You are indeed in your old error﴾ [Yusuf 12:95], meaning: your love. The meaning is that you were a lover, so I guided you to the laws by which one draws near to serving the Beloved.

The fifteenth: lost regarding the affairs of this world, not knowing trade and the like. Then I guided you until your trade prospered and your profit grew, so that Khadijah came to desire you. The meaning is that you had no grasp of this world, and you knew nothing but religion, so I guided you afterward to the interests of this world.

The sixteenth: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means: lost among your people, who used to harm you and would not accept you as a leader. So He strengthened your affair and guided you until you became a commander and ruler over them.

The seventeenth: you were lost, not guided on the path of the heavens, so I guided you when I ascended you to the heavens on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj).

The eighteenth: ﴿And He found you lost﴾, i.e., forgetful of His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:282]. So "I guided you", i.e., I reminded you. That is because on the night of the Ascension he forgot what should be said because of the awe, so God guided him to the manner of praise, until he said: "I cannot enumerate praise of You."

The nineteenth: although he knew God in his heart, outwardly he did not show them disagreement, so this was expressed as "going astray".

The twentieth: Ali, peace be upon him, narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I never intended anything of what the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to do, except twice, and each time God came between me and what I wished of it. After that I never intended any evil again, until God honoured me with His message. For I said one night to a young man of the Quraysh who was tending my sheep with me on the upper part of Makkah: 'If you would watch my sheep until I enter Makkah and spend the evening there as the young men do.' So I went out wanting that, until I came to the first house of the houses of Makkah, and I heard the sound of lutes and flutes. They said: 'So-and-so son of so-and-so is marrying so-and-so.' So I sat looking at them, and God struck my ears [with sleep], and I slept, and nothing woke me except the heat of the sun. He said: So I came to my companion, and he said: 'What did you do?' I said: 'I did nothing.' Then I told him the story. He said: Then I said to him another night like that, and God struck my ears, and nothing woke me except the heat of the sun. After that I never intended any evil again, until God, exalted is He, honoured me with His message."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 93, verse 8:

As for His saying, ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-'a'il* (the one who has 'ayla, poverty) is the one who has poverty. We mentioned this under His saying ﴿that you may not be unjust﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. The verse ﴿and if you fear poverty ('ayla)﴾ [al-Tawba: 28] also indicates this. Then *al-'a'il* is applied to the poor even if he has no dependents. Here there are two opinions regarding the interpretation of *al-'a'il*:

The first, which is the well-known view, is that it means the poor. This is supported by what is reported, that in the Mushaf (codex) of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads: "and He found you destitute (ʿadiman)," and it was recited as *ʿayyilan*, just as *sayyiʿat* was recited (with the doubled form). Then there are several ways in which He made him rich:

The first: Allah made him rich through the upbringing of Abu Talib. When Abu Talib's circumstances deteriorated, Allah made him rich through the wealth of Khadijah. When that also deteriorated, He made him rich through the wealth of Abu Bakr. When that also deteriorated, He commanded him to emigrate and made him rich through the support of the Ansar. Then He commanded him to fight (jihad) and made him rich through the spoils of war. Although this was obtained after the revelation of this surah, since it was known to occur, it was as if it had occurred. It is reported that he (peace be upon him) "entered upon Khadijah while he was distressed. She said to him, 'What is the matter with you?' He said, 'The time is a time of famine. If I spend the wealth, your wealth will be depleted and I will be ashamed before you; and if I do not spend, I fear Allah.' So she summoned the Quraysh, among whom was al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). Al-Siddiq said: She brought out dinars and poured them out until they reached an amount such that my sight did not fall upon those sitting in front of me because of the abundance of wealth. Then she said: Bear witness that this wealth is his; if he wishes he may distribute it, and if he wishes he may keep it.'"

The second: He made him rich through his companions, who used to worship Allah secretly, until Umar, when he embraced Islam, said: "Come out openly! Al-Lat is worshipped openly while we worship Allah in secret!" He (peace be upon him) said: "Not until the companions increase." Umar said: "Let Allah be sufficient for you and whoever follows you among the believers." [al-Anfal: 64] Then Allah made him rich through the wealth of Abu Bakr and through the awe inspired by Umar.

The third: He made you rich through contentment (qana'a), so that your state became one in which stone and gold were alike to you, and you find nothing in your heart but your Lord. Your Lord is rich independently of things, not through them, and you, through your contentment, became independent of things. The highest richness is independence from a thing, not through it. Among the evidence for this is that he (peace be upon him) was given the choice between wealth and poverty, and he chose poverty.

The fourth: You were destitute of proofs and arguments, so Allah sent down the Qur'an to you and taught you what you did not know, and so made you rich.

The second opinion regarding the interpretation of *al-'a'il*: You had many dependents, who are the Ummah, and so He sufficed you. It was also said: He made them rich through you, because they were poor due to their ignorance, while you were the possessor of knowledge, so He guided them by your hand. Here there are questions.

**The first question:** What is the wisdom in His choosing orphanhood for him? We say: there are several reasons:

One of them: that he would know the worth of orphans, so he would stand by their rights and the welfare of their affairs. Because of this, Yusuf (peace be upon him) would not be satiated. When he was asked about this, he said: "I fear that if I am satisfied I will forget the hungry."

The second: so that the orphan would share with him in the name, and thus be honored for that reason. Because of this he (peace be upon him) said: "When you name a child Muhammad, honor him and make room for him in the gathering."

The third: that whoever has a father or mother relies on them, so his parents were taken from him so that from the beginning of his childhood until the end of his life he would not rely on anyone other than Allah. Thus in his childhood he would resemble Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in his saying: "My knowledge of my condition is sufficient as a request," and like Maryam's reply: ﴿Where has this come to you? She said: It is from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37].

The fourth: it is customary that an orphan's faults are not concealed but become apparent, and people may exaggerate what exists. So Allah chose orphanhood for him so that everyone would examine his circumstances, and then they would find no fault in him, and they would agree on his purity. When Allah chose him for prophethood, they would find no ground for criticism against him.

The fifth: He made him an orphan so that everyone would know that his excellence came from Allah from the outset, because one who has a father, his father strives to teach and discipline him.

The sixth: poverty and orphanhood are deficiencies with respect to created beings. When Muhammad (peace be upon him) became, despite these two attributes, the most honorable of creation, this was a reversal of the custom, and so it was of the kind of miracles.

**The second question:** What is the wisdom in Allah mentioning these things? The answer: the wisdom is that he should not forget himself and fall into self-admiration (ʿujb).

**The third question:** It is reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "I asked my Lord a request which I wished I had not asked. I said: You took Ibrahim as a friend (khalil), You spoke to Musa directly, You subjected the mountains to Dawud, You gave Sulayman such-and-such, and You gave so-and-so such-and-such. He said: Did I not find you an orphan and shelter you? Did I not find you lost and guide you? Did I not find you poor and make you rich? I said: Yes. He said: Did I not open up your breast? I said: Yes. He said: Did I not raise your remembrance? I said: Yes. He said:

[p. 199]

Did I not remove from you your burden? I said: Yes. Did I not give you what I did not give any prophet before you, namely the last verses of Surat al-Baqara? Did I not take you as a friend (khalil) as I took Ibrahim as a friend?"

Is this hadith authentic? We say: al-Qadi criticized this report, saying: The prophets (peace be upon them) do not ask such a thing except with permission, so how could such a request proceed from the Messenger? And that which came from Him, the Exalted, would be in the manner of a reproach.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾. It is also read *fa-la takkhar* (فَلا تَكْهَرْ), meaning do not frown at him (لا تَعْبَسْ وجْهَكَ إلَيْهِ). The meaning is: deal with him in the same way that He dealt with you. A similar verse in some respect is ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 77]. From the same idea is his (peace be upon him) saying: "Allah, Allah regarding the one who has none but Allah."

It is narrated that it was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) shouted at the son of Khadijah. From the same idea is the hadith of Musa (peace be upon him) when he said: "My Lord, by what did I attain what I have attained?" He said: "Do you remember when the lamb fled from you, and when you caught up with it you said: 'You have tired yourself, then you carried it.' For this reason I made you a guardian over creation." When Musa (peace be upon him) attained prophethood through kindness to a sheep, how much more so through kindness to an orphan. And if this rebuke comes merely from shouting or frowning in the face, how much more so if he humiliates him or consumes his property.

From Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When an orphan weeps, his tears fall into the palm of the Most Merciful, and the Exalted says: Who made this orphan weep, whose father I covered with dust? Whoever silences him, for him is Paradise."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for the one who asks, do not repel him﴾. It is said: "nahara-hu" and "intahara-hu" mean that one confronts him with words that rebuke him.

Regarding who is meant by "the one who asks," there are two opinions.

The first, which is the choice of al-Hasan (al-Basri), is that it refers to one who asks for knowledge. A parallel to this in some respects is: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 1, 2]. In this case the sequence becomes coherent, because He first said to him: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And find you lost and guide you? And find you in need and make you self-sufficient?﴾ Then He considered this sequence and instructed him to care for the rights of the orphan, then to care for the rights of the one who asks him about knowledge and guidance, and then instructed him to give thanks for the blessings of God upon him.

The second opinion is that it refers to any questioner in general. God rebuked His Messenger in the Qur'an concerning the poor in three places:

The first: he "was sitting, and around him were the chieftains of Quraysh, when Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man, came, and he pushed through the necks of the people until he sat down in front of him, and said: 'Teach me of what God has taught you.' This was difficult for him, so his face frowned, and there was revealed: ﴿He frowned and turned away.﴾"

The second: when "Quraysh said to him: 'If you would make a gathering for us and a separate gathering for the poor,' he intended to do so, and then there was revealed His saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]."

The third: "He was sitting when ʿUthman came to him with a cluster of dates and placed it before him. He wanted to eat, when a beggar stood at the door and said: 'May God have mercy on a servant who has mercy on us.' So he ordered that it be given to the beggar. ʿUthman disliked this, and wanted the Prophet (ﷺ) to eat it, so he went out and bought it from the beggar. Then the beggar returned, and he did this three times, and the Prophet (ﷺ) kept giving it to him, until the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Are you a beggar or a seller?' Then there was revealed: ﴿As for the one who asks, do not repel him.﴾"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 93, verse 11:

Page 200
Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And as for the favor of your Lord, proclaim it﴾. In it there are several interpretations:

The first: Mujahid said: that favor is the Qur'an, for the Qur'an is the greatest of the blessings Allah bestowed upon Muhammad, peace be upon him, and proclaiming it means to recite it, to teach it to others, and to explain its realities to them.

The second: It is also narrated from Mujahid that the favor is prophethood, meaning: convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord.

The third: When Allah grants you success and you observe the rights of the orphan and the beggar, that success is a favor from Allah upon you, so proclaim it so that others may follow your example. From this is what is narrated from al-Husayn ibn Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: "When you know of some good, relate it to your brothers so that they may follow you." However, this is only good when it does not involve ostentation (riya') and when one believes that others will follow him. From this also is what is reported when the Commander of the Faithful Ali, peace be upon him, was asked about the Companions, and he praised them and mentioned their qualities. They said to him: "Then tell us about yourself." He said: "Enough, for Allah has forbidden self-praise (tazkiyah)." It was said to him: "Does not Allah, exalted is He, say: ﴿And as for the favor of your Lord, proclaim it﴾?" He said: "Indeed I do proclaim it. I used to give when asked, and when I was silent I would begin, and within my ribs is abundant knowledge, so ask me."

If it is asked: What is the wisdom in Allah, exalted is He, placing His own right after the right of the orphan and the needy? We say: there are several answers.

The first: It is as if He is saying: "I am self-sufficient, while they are in need, and giving precedence to the right of the one in need is more fitting."

The second: He placed the action in their share and was content for Himself with the speech.

The third: The purpose of all acts of worship is the absorption of the heart in the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. So He made the conclusion of these acts the heart's and tongue's recounting of the favors of Allah, exalted is He, so that the conclusion of the acts of worship is upon the remembrance of Allah. He chose His saying ﴿fa-haddith﴾ (then proclaim) over saying fa-khabbir (then inform), so that it would be a discourse that He keeps in mind and does not forget, repeating it time after time. And Allah knows best. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
